subject: ESS HL
title: Aster River Basin: Water Security and River Basin Management
summary: A fictional river basin used to investigate water security, competing water demands, pollution, stakeholder perspectives and sustainable river-basin management. All names and numerical data are hypothetical and created for examination practice.

resources.title: Resource 1: Basin background
resources.text: The Aster River rises in a forested upland, flows through an irrigated farming district and the city of Meridia, and then enters the internationally protected Luma Wetland. A reservoir upstream of Meridia supplies drinking water, irrigation water and hydropower. During the dry season, low river flow increases competition among users. The regional government is considering a new water-allocation plan that would cap irrigation withdrawals, expand wastewater treatment, introduce seasonal water pricing and guarantee a minimum environmental flow to the wetland.

resources.title: Resource 2: Annual freshwater withdrawals
resources.description: Hypothetical annual freshwater withdrawals in the Aster River Basin.
columns: 2032 projected withdrawal without new policy (million m³)
resources.note: Current long-term renewable freshwater availability is estimated at 760 million m³ per year.

resources.title: Resource 3: Mean monthly river discharge
resources.description: Mean monthly discharge measured downstream of Meridia in a representative year.
resources.note: Ecologists recommend that discharge should not fall below 30 m³ s⁻¹ for prolonged periods if wetland habitat quality is to be maintained.

resources.title: Resource 4: Water-quality survey
resources.description: Hypothetical mean water-quality measurements at three sampling sites.
resources.note: Higher BOD indicates greater oxygen demand by microorganisms decomposing biodegradable organic matter.

resources.title: Resource 5: Stakeholder positions
resources.text: Farmers argue that restricting irrigation could reduce crop yields and rural employment. Meridia's water utility supports higher dry-season prices because it expects demand management to postpone costly supply expansion. Wetland conservation groups support a legally guaranteed environmental flow and stronger nutrient controls. Some low-income urban residents oppose higher household water prices unless a basic water allowance is protected. The national government must also comply with a regional agreement requiring participating jurisdictions to avoid causing significant downstream environmental harm.

subject: ESS HL
title: Verdantia Forest Frontier: Biodiversity, Land Use and Food Production
summary: A fictional tropical forest frontier used to investigate habitat loss, biodiversity decline, agricultural expansion, soil degradation, conservation and sustainable food production. All names and numerical data are hypothetical and created for examination practice.

resources.title: Resource 1: Landscape background
resources.text: The fictional Verdantia Forest Frontier covers 100,000 hectares of lowland tropical landscape. During the last two decades, road construction and export-oriented soybean production have expanded into native forest. The remaining forest contains several endemic bird and amphibian species and provides water regulation, soil protection, carbon storage and pollination services. The government is considering a land-use strategy that would prohibit further clearance in high-biodiversity forest, establish an 8,000-hectare wildlife corridor between two protected areas, charge a levy on high fertilizer use and pay farmers who convert part of their land to agroforestry.

resources.title: Resource 2: Land-use change in Verdantia
resources.description: Hypothetical land-use areas in 2005 and 2025. The total landscape area is 100,000 ha in both years.
resources.note: Most new soybean fields and roads were established in areas that were native forest in 2005.

resources.title: Resource 3: Forest-specialist bird population index
resources.description: A hypothetical index based on repeated surveys of forest-specialist birds. The index is set to 100 in 2005.
resources.note: Survey methods were kept consistent between years. The index represents relative abundance rather than the number of species.

resources.title: Resource 4: Comparison of farming systems
resources.description: Hypothetical mean values from farms with similar rainfall and soil parent material.
resources.note: Yield values are not directly equivalent in market value because the systems produce different combinations of products.

resources.title: Resource 5: Stakeholder positions
resources.text: An agribusiness association argues that soybean expansion provides export earnings, tax revenue and employment and warns that strict land limits could reduce investment. Conservation organizations support the corridor and a permanent ban on clearing high-biodiversity forest because fragmented populations may become isolated. A smallholder cooperative supports payments for agroforestry but opposes rules that could remove productive land without compensation. Indigenous communities downstream emphasize the cultural value of intact forest and clean water. The government states that its goal is to maintain food production while preventing further biodiversity loss and soil degradation.

subject: ESS HL
title: Kestrel Republic: Energy Transition, Climate Policy and Urban Air Quality
summary: A fictional national energy transition used to investigate fossil-fuel dependence, renewable energy, greenhouse-gas mitigation, urban air pollution, energy security and social equity. All names and numerical data are hypothetical and created for examination practice.

resources.title: Resource 1: National energy background
resources.text: The fictional Kestrel Republic has historically generated most of its electricity from domestic coal and imported natural gas. Coal mining provides employment in two inland provinces, while the capital, Aurum City, experiences frequent winter air-pollution episodes. The government has proposed a 2035 energy-transition plan that would retire the oldest coal plants, expand solar and wind generation, add grid-scale storage, introduce a carbon price, strengthen power-station air-pollution controls and provide retraining and income support for workers in coal-dependent communities. A protected basic electricity tariff would remain available for low-income households.

resources.title: Resource 2: Electricity generation mix
resources.description: Hypothetical annual electricity generation in 2025 and under the government's 2035 plan.
resources.note: The plan assumes total electricity demand rises because of economic growth and electrification of transport and heating.

resources.title: Resource 3: Operational emissions from electricity sources
resources.description: Hypothetical average operational emissions. Values exclude construction, fuel extraction and other life-cycle emissions.
resources.note: Zero values indicate no direct operational combustion emissions; they do not imply zero life-cycle environmental impact.

resources.title: Resource 4: Annual mean PM2.5 concentration in Aurum City
resources.description: Hypothetical citywide annual mean PM2.5 concentration under the government's transition scenario.
resources.note: The national policy target is to reduce the annual mean below 25 µg m⁻³ by 2035. Transport, industry and household fuels also contribute to Aurum City's PM2.5, so changes cannot be attributed to the electricity sector alone.

resources.title: Resource 5: Stakeholder positions
resources.text: Coal-worker unions support cleaner air but argue that plant closures should occur only after credible replacement jobs and income protection are available. Renewable-energy companies support faster auctions for solar, wind and storage. Energy-intensive manufacturers worry that carbon pricing could raise electricity costs and reduce international competitiveness. Public-health organizations support rapid coal retirement because lower particulate and sulfur emissions could reduce respiratory and cardiovascular disease. Climate groups argue that the transition should be faster because electricity-sector decarbonization can also support low-carbon transport and heating. The government argues that domestic renewable generation will reduce dependence on imported gas and improve long-term energy security.

subject: ESS HL
title: Nova Metro Region: Urban Growth, Waste Management and Air Quality
summary: A fictional metropolitan region used to investigate urbanization, municipal solid waste, transport, air pollution, circularity, urban planning and social equity. All names and numerical data are hypothetical and created for examination practice.

resources.title: Resource 1: Metropolitan background
resources.text: The fictional Nova Metro Region has grown rapidly as people move from surrounding rural districts and smaller towns. Housing expansion has spread beyond the original urban boundary, traffic congestion has increased and the main landfill is approaching capacity. The metropolitan authority proposes a 2035 strategy that combines higher-density transit-oriented development, expanded bus and rail services, a low-emission zone, separate collection of organic waste, more recycling, anaerobic digestion and composting, landfill methane capture, urban green infrastructure and upgraded waste collection in informal settlements. The authority states that the strategy should reduce pollution without making housing, transport or waste services less affordable for low-income residents.

resources.title: Resource 2: Population and municipal solid waste
resources.description: Hypothetical population and municipal solid-waste generation in Nova Metro Region.
resources.note: The 2035 waste value is a projection without additional waste-prevention measures.

resources.title: Resource 3: Waste-management mix
resources.description: Hypothetical shares of municipal solid waste by treatment route.
resources.note: The strategy also includes landfill-methane capture. Percentages sum to 100 in each year.

resources.title: Resource 4: Urban transport and air quality
resources.description: Hypothetical transport-mode shares and annual mean roadside PM2.5 concentration.
resources.note: Road traffic is not the only source of PM2.5; industry, construction and household fuels also contribute.

resources.title: Resource 5: Stakeholder positions
resources.text: Public-transport users support more frequent and reliable services but oppose fare increases. Residents near the landfill support reduced disposal and methane capture because of odour and air-quality concerns. Informal waste pickers fear losing livelihoods if recycling becomes centralized, while environmental groups argue that waste prevention, reuse and recycling should remain above incineration in the waste hierarchy. Developers support transit-oriented construction but warn that stricter land-use rules may increase housing costs. Public-health organizations support the low-emission zone. Community groups in informal settlements argue that universal waste collection and affordable transport should be implemented before penalties or service charges are increased.

subject: ESS HL
title: Bluehaven Lake and Delta: Fisheries, Aquaculture and Water Quality
summary: A fictional freshwater lake and delta system used to investigate capture fisheries, aquaculture, eutrophication, water pollution, resource management and stakeholder trade-offs. All names and numerical data are hypothetical and created for examination practice.

resources.title: Resource 1: Lake and delta background
resources.text: Bluehaven is a fictional freshwater lake connected to a shallow delta lagoon. The lake supports a commercial wild fishery, small-scale fishing communities and a rapidly expanding cage-aquaculture industry. Crop farms and settlements in the catchment add nutrients to inflowing rivers. The government is considering a management package that would reduce fishing effort, introduce catch quotas, create a seasonal no-take spawning zone, tighten aquaculture nutrient-discharge permits, restore riparian buffer vegetation and upgrade wastewater treatment. Fish farmers argue that aquaculture is needed to maintain food supply as wild catches decline, while fishing communities are concerned about both stock decline and restrictions on access.

resources.title: Resource 2: Fisheries and aquaculture indicators
resources.description: Hypothetical indicators for Bluehaven Lake.
resources.note: Fishing effort combines vessel number, fishing days and gear capacity into one relative index.

resources.title: Resource 3: Water-quality survey
resources.description: Hypothetical annual mean values at three monitoring sites.
resources.note: Higher chlorophyll-a is used here as an indicator of greater phytoplankton biomass. Measurements show association, not proof of a single pollution source.

resources.title: Resource 4: Aquaculture nutrient-loss scenarios
resources.description: Hypothetical nutrient losses per tonne of fish produced.
resources.note: The 2026 aquaculture output is 38,000 tonnes yr⁻¹. Values exclude nutrient inputs from farms, settlements and natural sources.

resources.title: Resource 5: Stakeholder positions and proposed management
resources.text: Commercial fishers support rebuilding wild stocks but oppose abrupt quota cuts that could reduce income. Small-scale fishing communities request priority access near villages and financial support during the spawning closure. Aquaculture companies support improved feed but argue that closed recirculating systems are too costly for rapid adoption. Delta conservation groups want stricter nutrient limits because low dissolved oxygen threatens fish, invertebrates and wetland biodiversity. Farmers upstream oppose a nutrient levy unless grants are available for riparian buffers and more efficient fertilizer use. The government proposes a five-year package combining a 20% reduction in fishing effort, science-based catch quotas, a seasonal no-take spawning zone, improved-feed standards for cages, nutrient-discharge permits, riparian buffers and upgraded wastewater treatment.

subject: ESS HL
title: Maruva Plains: Soil Degradation, Food Security and Climate Resilience
summary: A fictional semi-arid agricultural region used to investigate soil degradation, erosion, salinization, soil organic matter, food security, climate pressure and sustainable land management. All names and numerical data are hypothetical and created for examination practice.

resources.title: Resource 1: Regional background
resources.text: The fictional Maruva Plains are a semi-arid cereal-producing region where farming has expanded onto marginal land as population and food demand have grown. Many fields are repeatedly tilled and left bare between crops, while livestock graze communal dry-season pastures. Irrigated districts have experienced rising soil salinity. Farmers also report less reliable growing-season rainfall and more extreme heat. The government proposes a 2035 soil-and-food resilience programme combining reduced tillage, cover crops, contour farming, compost and manure additions, rotational grazing, more efficient irrigation and drainage, drought-tolerant crop varieties, soil-monitoring services and transition grants for smallholders.

resources.title: Resource 2: Agricultural and soil indicators
resources.description: Hypothetical regional indicators for Maruva Plains.
resources.note: Cultivated area increased partly through expansion onto more erosion-prone marginal land.

resources.title: Resource 3: Growing-season climate indicators
resources.description: Hypothetical regional climate indicators. Three dates alone do not establish attribution to a single cause.
resources.note: Year-to-year variability remains high, but farmers report increasing concern about drought and heat stress.

resources.title: Resource 4: Farm-management trial
resources.description: Hypothetical five-year mean results from comparable fields.
resources.note: The trial does not include full transition costs, labour requirements or every possible crop-year condition.

resources.title: Resource 5: Stakeholder positions and proposed programme
resources.text: Smallholder groups support soil restoration but say equipment, cover-crop seed and short-term transition costs are unaffordable without grants or credit. Large commercial farms support irrigation-efficiency measures but oppose strict limits on fertilizer or cultivated area. Pastoralist groups support rotational grazing if access to traditional dry-season water points is protected. Consumer organizations are concerned that declining regional production could raise staple-food prices. Soil scientists support reduced tillage, organic-matter restoration and contour measures because they can reduce erosion and improve water retention. The government proposes grants targeted to smallholders, extension services, salinity-control drainage, efficient irrigation, drought-tolerant varieties and payments for verified improvements in soil cover and soil organic matter.

subject: ESS HL
title: Talaris Highlands: Critical Minerals, Mining and Environmental Justice
summary: A fictional critical-mineral mining proposal used to investigate resource extraction, water use, pollution risk, biodiversity, environmental law, ecological economics, ethics and environmental justice. All names and numerical data are hypothetical and created for examination practice.

resources.title: Resource 1: Mining proposal background
resources.text: The fictional Talaris Highlands contain a nickel-bearing hard-rock deposit. Nickel from the proposed mine would be sold for batteries, grid storage and other low-carbon infrastructure. A three-year exploration and pilot-processing programme has already operated on a small area. The proposed full mine would operate for 20 years near montane forest, peat-rich wet meadows and headwater streams used by downstream communities. The company argues that the project would support the energy transition, employment and public revenue. Local Indigenous communities and conservation groups argue that climate benefits elsewhere do not automatically justify local water, habitat and cultural losses. The government is deciding whether to approve the mine under an enhanced-safeguards permit.

resources.title: Resource 2: Proposed mine material, economic and water indicators
resources.description: Hypothetical annual indicators for the proposed full mine.
rows: Water recycled with enhanced closed-loop system
Share of royalty transferred to affected municipalities
resources.note: Gross nickel value is before operating, financing, rehabilitation and other costs. Price and production are held constant only for examination calculations.

resources.title: Resource 3: Pilot-area water-quality survey
resources.description: Hypothetical mean values from monitoring during the small pilot-processing programme.
resources.note: The data show spatial association during the pilot period but do not by themselves prove the source of every water-quality difference or predict full-mine conditions.

resources.title: Resource 4: Full-mine design alternatives
resources.description: Hypothetical comparison of the company's base design and an enhanced-safeguards design required by regulators.
resources.note: The enhanced design reroutes infrastructure around sensitive habitat and uses more water recycling. The no-mine alternative would avoid these local impacts and jobs but would not remove global demand for nickel; extraction could occur elsewhere.

resources.title: Resource 5: Governance, economics, ethics and stakeholder positions
resources.text: Under fictional Talaris environmental law, a full permit requires an environmental impact assessment, public disclosure of monitoring data, a rehabilitation bond paid before production and enforceable water-quality conditions. The government proposes a 5% mineral royalty, with 30% of royalty revenue transferred to affected municipalities, plus a biodiversity no-net-loss requirement using avoidance, restoration and offsets. The Indigenous Highlands Council asks for co-management of water monitoring, protection of sacred headwaters and the right to reject mine infrastructure in specified cultural zones. The company accepts the rehabilitation bond and independent monitoring but argues that larger exclusion zones could reduce ore access, jobs and tax revenue. Conservation groups invoke the precautionary principle because some headwater and wetland damage may be difficult to reverse. Economists note that employment and royalty revenue are market benefits, while pollution, habitat loss and cultural damage can be external costs unless they are prevented, compensated or internalized. Climate-transition groups support responsible nickel production but argue that recycling, material efficiency and lower-consumption pathways should reduce the need for continual expansion of primary extraction.

subject: ESS HL
title: Selene Coast: Sea-Level Rise, Coastal Biodiversity and Adaptation
summary: A fictional low-lying coast used to investigate sea-level rise, coastal ecosystems, biodiversity, flood risk, adaptation, environmental governance and environmental justice. All names and numerical data are hypothetical and created for examination practice.

resources.title: Resource 1: Coastal background
resources.text: The fictional Selene Coast is a low-lying estuary containing mangrove forest, salt marsh, tidal flats, beaches and growing coastal settlements. The ecosystems provide nursery habitat, shoreline stabilization, carbon storage, recreation and storm-wave attenuation. Since 2005, tourism development, roads and housing have restricted the landward migration of some wetlands. Higher relative sea level and more frequent high-water flooding are increasing risk to homes, a port, wastewater infrastructure and coastal habitats. The regional government is considering a 2050 adaptation pathway combining wetland restoration, living shorelines, development setbacks, elevated infrastructure, targeted seawalls, voluntary buyouts and managed retreat from the most exposed zones.

resources.title: Resource 2: Coastal change and exposure
resources.description: Hypothetical indicators for Selene Coast.
rows: Mean annual flood damage (US$ million yr⁻¹)
resources.note: Changes reflect multiple drivers, including development, shoreline modification, storms and sea-level rise.

resources.title: Resource 3: Relative sea level and high-water flooding
resources.description: Hypothetical observed values to 2025 and a planning scenario for 2050.
resources.note: The 2050 values are a planning scenario, not a certain prediction. Relative sea level includes both ocean-level change and local land movement.

resources.title: Resource 4: Adaptation strategy comparison
resources.description: Hypothetical 2050 planning estimates.
columns: Estimated annual flood damage avoided (US$ million yr⁻¹)
rows: Hybrid: living shorelines + setbacks + targeted seawalls
resources.note: Values exclude many non-market ecosystem services, maintenance costs, future property-price changes and uncertainty in storm frequency.

resources.title: Resource 5: Governance and stakeholder positions
resources.text: Under fictional Selene coastal law, major shoreline projects require climate-risk assessment, public consultation and avoidance of significant damage to protected tidal wetlands where feasible. The government proposes a coastal adaptation fund financed by general revenue and a levy on large waterfront tourism properties. Low-income residents of Bayview support flood protection but fear that buyouts, rising insurance costs or redevelopment could displace established communities. Fishing groups support mangrove and marsh restoration because these habitats support juvenile fish. Waterfront property owners favour seawalls and oppose mandatory setbacks without compensation. Conservation scientists argue that fixed seawalls can cause coastal squeeze where wetlands cannot migrate inland. An Indigenous coastal council seeks protection of cultural sites and co-management of restored wetlands. Economists note that avoided flood losses are only part of total benefit because wetlands also provide ecosystem services that may not be fully priced. The government proposes compensation, affordable-housing protections, rolling development setbacks, independent monitoring and five-year adaptation reviews.
